title: The Commercial Holiday Decorating Timeline for Ontario Properties
metaDescription: Month-by-month timeline for commercial holiday decorating in Ontario: booking, site visits, install windows, maintenance, January takedown and storage.
excerpt: A month-by-month guide to how commercial holiday decorating actually runs in Ontario, from summer site visits and design to October and November installs, season-long maintenance, January takedown and warehouse storage. Written for property managers, hotel GMs and BIA coordinators who need to book dates early.

sections.heading: Why the calendar matters more than the budget
paragraphs: Most commercial holiday decorating problems are not design problems or budget problems. They are calendar problems. A property that calls in the second week of November is choosing from the dates and the inventory that are left, not from the full range. A property that books in July gets first pick of install dates, the trees it wants and a crew that is not rushing.

Our season has a fixed shape. Site visits and design happen from July to September. Installs run from October to late November so displays are lit before Black Friday. Maintenance runs through the holidays. Takedown fills the first three weeks of January. Storage and rebooking happen through the winter and spring. Everything we do is planned around that shape.

This guide walks through the year month by month so you can see where your property fits. If you manage a hotel, an office tower, a condo lobby, a plaza or a downtown BIA, the dates are the same. What changes is how much lead time your approvals need, and that is usually the part people underestimate.

sections.heading: The year at a glance
paragraphs: Here is the full cycle in one table. The install and takedown windows are set by weather, daylight and the retail calendar. The planning windows in front of them are set by how long it takes to measure a property, design a scheme, get it approved and reserve product. Properties with boards or head-office sign-off should add a month to every planning step.

Use this table to work backwards from the date you want the display lit. If that date is the week before Black Friday, your install needs to be booked by early autumn and your site visit done in summer. If you are flexible on the lit date, you have more room, but the best install slots still go first.

sections.heading: Summer: site visits, design and the approval clock
paragraphs: The site visit is where a commercial program is really designed. We measure linear footage on rooflines and canopies, count and size the trees you want wrapped, check lobby ceiling height and floor space for a tree, look for outlets and note where a bucket truck or aerial lift can park. It takes 30 to 60 minutes and saves weeks of back and forth later.

From the site visit we produce a proposal with the scope, the product we will supply from our own inventory, the install window and the full program: installation, maintenance, January takedown and storage. For lobby trees and large displays we usually recommend leasing per season, and the proposal explains the lease and purchase options side by side.

Approvals are the hidden delay. A condo board may only meet monthly. A hotel may need head-office sign-off on brand colours. A BIA may need a vote. Build that time in. Our target is to have agreements signed and deposits in by the end of September so product is reserved and install dates are locked before October begins.
bullets: Bring the person who will approve the budget to the site walk if you can.
Have last year's photos handy, even if you want something different.
Tell us about events, grand openings or inspections that fix a lit-by date.

sections.heading: October: exterior installs start
paragraphs: October is when the bucket trucks and aerial lifts go out. Exterior work goes first because it is weather dependent and because rooflines, columns, porte-cochères and wrapped trees take the most crew hours. Installing in October means the work is done in milder weather and daylight, and the display simply stays off on the timer until you want it lit.

Properties that insist on a late install often end up paying for it in a different way: rushed crews, fewer date choices and a display that goes up in sleet. Our commercial-grade LED strings and C9 bulbs are built to sit on a roofline through winter, so there is no downside to installing early and lighting later.

After-hours and overnight installs are normal in October for hotels, condos and plazas. We agree a window with your building staff, cone off only the area we are working in, and keep guest arrivals, deliveries and parking moving. If a property has light daytime traffic, a daytime install is faster and we will say so.

sections.heading: November: lobbies, atriums and the Black Friday deadline
paragraphs: Interior work fills November. Pre-lit lobby trees from 7 to 20 feet, elevator-lobby trees, staircase and railing garland, entrance arches, wreaths and planters go in once the exterior is done. Interior installs are usually overnight for hotels and shopping centres so guests and shoppers arrive to a finished display, and after hours for office towers and condos.

The deadline that drives the month is late November. Retail properties want to be lit before Black Friday. Hotels want the lobby done before holiday party season starts. Office towers want tenants to walk in to a decorated lobby on the first of December. We schedule to hit those dates, which is why early booking matters so much.

The last thing the crew does on every install is test every circuit, set every timer and walk the display with you or your staff. You get a contact for the season. From that point, the display is our responsibility to keep lit. Staff do not need to switch anything on or off, and timer changes for a tenant event are one phone call.

sections.heading: December: maintenance you should not have to think about
paragraphs: Season-long maintenance is included in every program at no charge for any fault. In practice that means a tripped GFCI, a timer knocked out of sync after the time change, a plug pulled by a snowplow or a tree section that goes dark gets fixed when you call. On larger programs we also do our own drive-by checks so many faults are fixed before anyone notices.

Because everything is our own inventory, the truck carries matching replacement strings, bulbs and timers. There is no waiting for a part or arguing about whose product failed. That is the main reason we do not install customer-supplied lights: we cannot warranty product we did not source and test. It also means repairs match the rest of the display instead of standing out.

December is also when properties ask for small changes: lights on later for a tenant event, a tree moved for a photo day, a wreath added at a side entrance. Timer changes are part of the program. Design changes are quoted separately and done quickly. Tell us a day ahead where you can and we will fit it into the route.

sections.heading: January: takedown, labelling and storage
paragraphs: Takedown runs through the first three weeks of January. The same crews with the same lifts remove the display, after hours where needed, and pack everything by property and location. Exterior strings are tested, coiled and tagged by run. Lobby trees come down in sections. Ornaments and ribbon are boxed so the same scheme can go back up next year without a redesign.

Everything goes to our warehouse. Labelled storage is included whether you lease the decor or own it and pay for the service program. You get your mechanical room and storage cage back and nobody on your staff has to carry boxes to a basement. If you want plain warm-white lighting kept up as winter lighting into February or March, tell us at quoting time and we plan the takedown around it.

Takedown is also when we note what to improve: a roofline that needs an outlet added, a tree that has outgrown its wrap, a lobby that could take a taller tree. Those notes go into your file for next season's proposal. By the time we meet in summer, the plan for the coming season is already half written.

sections.heading: Winter and spring: rebooking and multi-year agreements
paragraphs: Returning clients get priority dates the next season. A multi-year agreement goes further: it locks pricing and the install and takedown schedule for the term, reserves your product in our warehouse and lets you set the holiday budget once. For hotels, property management portfolios and BIAs that need a predictable number every year, this is the simplest way to run the program.

If you want to change the look, late winter is the time to say so. A refresh on a leased lobby tree, from gold and warm white to blue and silver for example, is a design change rather than a purchase. Adding scope, such as wrapping more boulevard trees or lighting a second entrance, is quoted as an addition while the rest of the agreement stays as is.

Call 519-266-6796 or send a request and we reply within one business day. The earlier in the year you start, the more of this timeline works in your favour. If you are reading this in July, you are right on time. If you are reading it in November, call anyway and we will tell you what is still possible this season and hold your dates for the next.

faqs.question: What is the latest we can book commercial Christmas lights in Ontario?
faqs.answer: We take requests into November when crew capacity allows, but choice of dates and inventory is narrow by then. For a display lit before Black Friday, aim to sign by the end of September. For a lobby tree only, October is often still workable. Call and we will tell you honestly what is possible.

faqs.question: Can the lights be installed in October but not turned on until December?
faqs.answer: Yes, and this is how most of our exterior programs run. Commercial-grade LED strings and C9 bulbs are built to sit on a roofline through winter. We install in milder weather, set the timers and leave the display off until the date you choose. There is no extra cost for lighting later.

faqs.question: When are commercial Christmas decorations taken down?
faqs.answer: Takedown runs through the first three weeks of January. We can hold a specific date if you have an event or want the lobby back on a certain day. Plain warm-white lighting can stay up as winter lighting into February or March if you ask at quoting time.

title: Lease vs Buy: Commercial Christmas Decor Explained
metaDescription: Lease or buy commercial Christmas decor? An honest comparison of turnkey seasonal leasing and purchase-plus-service programs for Ontario properties.
excerpt: An honest comparison of the two ways commercial properties pay for holiday decor: a turnkey seasonal lease that bundles design, product, install, maintenance, removal and storage, or buying the product and paying for the service program each year. Which fits your building, your budget and your plans.

sections.heading: Two ways to pay for the same display
paragraphs: Every commercial holiday decor program has the same parts: a design, the product, the installation, maintenance through the season, takedown in January and somewhere to keep it all until next year. What changes between leasing and buying is who owns the product and how the cost is spread across years.

With turnkey commercial Christmas decor leasing, you pay one price per season and the product stays ours. With buying, you own the trees, lights, ornaments and ribbon, and you pay us each year for the service program: install, maintenance, takedown and storage. Both are legitimate. We offer both. Which one fits depends on how long you plan to keep the look, how much you want to spend in year one and how much you value flexibility.

This guide explains both honestly, including where buying wins. For lobby trees and large displays, leasing is our default recommendation, and we explain why below. For some exterior programs, buying can make sense. Either way, the installation, maintenance, takedown and storage are the same crews doing the same work. The only difference is who owns what is on the truck.

sections.heading: What a seasonal lease includes
paragraphs: A lease bundles everything into a single seasonal price and a single invoice. Design from a site visit. Product from our own commercial-grade inventory. Installation by insured, WSIB-compliant crews with bucket trucks and aerial lifts, after hours or overnight where needed. Maintenance all season at no charge for any fault. January takedown. Labelled storage in our warehouse. Priority dates the following season.

Because the product stays ours, we carry the risk on it. If a tree section fails, a string goes dark or ribbon fades, it is replaced from our stock and it is our problem. You never store boxes in a mechanical room, ask a superintendent to test strings or wonder whether a five-year-old tree will light this year.

A lease also makes change easy. Refreshing a lobby tree from warm white and gold to blue and silver is a design change, not a purchase. Scaling the program up or down is a conversation at renewal. Multi-year lease agreements lock the price and the dates so budgeting is simple.
bullets: One seasonal price, one invoice, nothing to own or store
Product risk stays with us and is covered by included maintenance
Colour scheme and scope can change between seasons

sections.heading: What buying plus a service program includes
paragraphs: When you buy, you purchase the product from our inventory outright: lobby trees, ornaments, ribbon, garland, wreaths, exterior strings, C9 bulbs, cone trees and so on. You then pay each year for the service program. That program is the same work as a lease without the product: installation, season-long maintenance, January takedown and labelled storage in our warehouse.

Year one costs more because you are paying for product and service together. Later years cost less than an equivalent lease because you are only paying for service. If you keep the same look for several seasons and the product is cared for, the total over four or five years can be lower than leasing.

The trade-offs are real. Changing the scheme means buying new ribbon and ornaments. Product ages, and while our commercial-grade LED product lasts well, owners do eventually face replacement. And if the property changes hands or the program is cancelled, you own decor you may not need. We still only install product that came from our inventory, because that is what we can warranty.
bullets: Higher year-one cost, lower cost in later years if the look stays the same
You own the product and its ageing
Design changes mean buying new pieces

sections.heading: Side by side
paragraphs: The table below is the way we explain the choice on a site visit. It is not a sales pitch for one side. Some properties are better off buying, usually those with a fixed exterior program and a long-term owner. Most lobby and atrium programs, and most hotels, are better off leasing.

Read the rows about flexibility and risk as carefully as the rows about cost. The cheapest option over five years is not the cheapest option if you change the scheme in year three or the building changes ownership in year two. Finance teams tend to look at the first two rows. Operations teams should look at the last four.

sections.heading: Why leasing is our default for lobby trees and large displays
paragraphs: A pre-lit lobby tree is a large, specialised piece of product. A 12 to 20 foot commercial tree is heavy, comes in many sections, needs testing every year and takes real storage space. Ornaments and ribbon for a tree that size are a significant cost on their own and are the first thing clients want to change when they tire of a look.

Leasing puts all of that on us. We store it, test it, replace failed sections and refresh the scheme when you want. The property gets a finished lobby every year for a predictable price and never deals with the product. For hotels and office towers where the lobby is the brand, that reliability is the point.

Mall village displays, Santa photo sets, giant outdoor trees and animated pixel light shows are the same story at larger scale. Owning a Santa cabin that you use for six weeks and store for forty-six rarely makes sense. Leasing it does. The same goes for animated pixel light shows, where the controllers and the programming are part of what you are leasing.

sections.heading: When buying can be the better choice
paragraphs: Buying makes the most sense for a fixed exterior program on a property with a stable owner and no plans to change the look. A plaza that wants warm-white rooflines and wrapped parking-lot trees every year, a church with an outlined roofline, or a restaurant with a lit patio and cone trees can buy once and pay for service each year.

It can also suit organisations whose budgets favour capital spending over operating spending, or municipalities and BIAs that must own assets bought with certain funds. We will quote both options so your finance team can compare them on the same scope. Ask for both numbers and let the people who manage the money choose.

The one thing we do not do is install product you bought elsewhere. Everything on a roofline or in a lobby under our name is from our inventory, tested by us and covered by our maintenance. That is how we can promise no charge for any fault during the season. If you are switching from another supplier, we will tell you honestly what can be retired.

sections.heading: How to decide for your property
paragraphs: Ask three questions. How long will the look stay the same? If the honest answer is two or three seasons, lease. How stable is the ownership and the budget line? If the property may change hands or the program may be cut, lease. Is the display mostly interior or display pieces? If yes, lease. If the answer to all three points the other way, buying is worth pricing.

Whichever you choose, the program around it is the same: site visit and design in summer, install from October to late November, maintenance all season, takedown in January, storage in our warehouse and priority dates next year. Multi-year agreements are available for both models and lock pricing and schedule. Only the ownership line on the invoice changes.

Call 519-266-6796 or send a request and we will quote both options from a site visit or from plans and photos, with a reply within one business day. Bring last year's invoice if you have one. Seeing what you paid for product and service separately is the fastest way to tell which model fits your property, and we will walk through it with you on the site visit.

faqs.question: Is leasing commercial Christmas decor cheaper than buying?
faqs.answer: In year one, yes. Over four or five seasons with no changes to the look, buying plus a service program can total less. Leasing wins on flexibility and risk because the product, its ageing and its storage are ours. For lobby trees and large displays we recommend leasing.

faqs.question: Can we switch from leasing to buying later?
faqs.answer: Yes. Some clients lease for a season or two to settle on a scheme, then buy the product they want to keep and move to the service program. We quote the switch at renewal and the install, maintenance, takedown and storage carry on as before.

faqs.question: Will you install decorations we already own?
faqs.answer: No. We only install product from our own inventory because that is what we can test, warranty and replace at no charge during the season. If you have existing decor, we can advise on what to retire and quote a replacement program that is covered.

title: How to Choose the Right Lobby Christmas Tree Size
metaDescription: Lobby Christmas tree size guide for commercial buildings: tree height vs ceiling height, footprint, sight lines, elevator lobbies and atriums, 7 to 20+ ft.
excerpt: How to size a commercial lobby Christmas tree so it fills the space without crowding it. Ceiling clearance, footprint, sight lines from the entrance, elevator lobbies, double-height lobbies and atriums, with a height-to-ceiling table and the questions we ask on every site visit.

sections.heading: The most common mistake is going too small
paragraphs: A lobby Christmas tree that is too small reads as an afterthought. A 7 foot tree in a double-height marble lobby looks like someone brought it from home. Commercial spaces have higher ceilings, longer sight lines and more hard surfaces than a living room, and the tree has to hold its own against all of that.

The opposite mistake, a tree that touches the ceiling or blocks the path to the elevators, is rarer but worse, because it is a safety and access problem rather than a style problem. The right size sits between the two and is decided by four things: ceiling height, floor space, sight lines and how the space is used.

Our pre-lit lobby trees run from 7 feet to 20 feet and beyond for atriums. This guide explains how we choose, with the same table we use on site visits, so you can walk your own lobby with a tape measure before we arrive. Photos of your lobby and a ceiling height are enough for a first suggestion.

sections.heading: Start with ceiling height
paragraphs: Measure from the floor to the lowest obstruction above the spot where the tree will stand. That might be a ceiling, a soffit, a light fixture, a sprinkler head or a sign. Then subtract clearance. We leave at least 18 inches between the topper and the ceiling so the tree does not look jammed in and so there is room to set and remove the top section.

Remember that the tree stands on a base, and some bases sit in a decorative collar or planter that adds a few inches. The height we quote is the finished height including the base and any topper, so there is no surprise on install day. Toppers add 12 to 18 inches on larger trees, which is why the clearance rule matters.

Use the table below as a starting point. It assumes a standard full-profile commercial tree with a topper and a collar at the base. Slim-profile trees follow the same height rule with a footprint about a third smaller, which is often the answer in a narrow lobby. Where two heights are listed, the taller one suits a lobby with a clear centre and the shorter one suits a busy or furnished lobby.

rows: Elevator lobby, reception, small condo lobby
Standard office or condo lobby, hotel reception

sections.heading: Floor space and the path around the tree
paragraphs: Tree width is roughly half to two thirds of its height on a full-profile tree. A 12 foot tree is about 7 to 8 feet across at the bottom. Add a skirt, collar or a ring of lit gift boxes and you need a clear circle of 9 or 10 feet. That circle has to leave room for people to pass, doors to swing, and any accessibility routes to stay open.

Measure the clear floor area where the tree will stand and think about how people move through it at 8:30 on a weekday morning. A tree that sits beautifully in an empty lobby on a Sunday can be a bottleneck when tenants arrive. In tight lobbies a slim-profile tree keeps the height while cutting the footprint by a third.

We also keep trees clear of sprinkler heads, fire pull stations, exits and security sight lines from the desk to the doors. If the only spot that works is smaller than the tree you want, two or three smaller trees in a group often give more presence than one compromised tall tree.
bullets: Clear circle needed is roughly tree width plus 2 feet
Keep accessibility routes and exits fully open
Slim-profile trees keep height with less footprint

sections.heading: Sight lines from the entrance
paragraphs: Stand at the front door and look in. The tree should be visible as soon as someone enters, ideally centred on the main axis of the lobby or placed where the eye lands naturally, such as beside the elevators or against a feature wall. A tall tree hidden behind a column does not do its job.

Glass lobbies work both ways: the tree is also seen from the street at night. In a floor-to-ceiling glass office lobby, a warm-white tree with gold ribbon placed near the glass becomes exterior decor as well, which is worth considering when you are comparing it against the cost of roofline lighting.

Sight lines also decide how much of the tree needs to be decorated. A tree against a wall can be decorated on the visible sides. A tree in the centre of an atrium is seen from every angle and from upper floors, so it is decorated all the way round and the topper matters more.

sections.heading: Elevator lobbies, reception desks and secondary trees
paragraphs: Secondary trees carry the scheme from the front door through the building. A 7 to 9 foot tree in the elevator lobby, a pair of lit accent trees flanking the main tree, or potted lit trees at the entrance in gold planters all extend the display without needing another tall ceiling.

Elevator lobbies are often the tightest spaces in the building. Ceiling heights drop, doors open into the space and there is a lot of foot traffic. A slim 7 foot tree in a corner, or lit gift boxes beside the elevators, usually works better than a full-profile tree. Match the ribbon and ornaments to the main tree so the whole route reads as one design.

Reception desks and staircases take garland rather than trees. Lit garland along a railing or across the front of a desk, with the same ribbon and accents as the tree, finishes the lobby at a fraction of the cost of a second tall tree. Garland is also the easiest piece to add in a later season without a redesign.

sections.heading: Atriums and double-height lobbies
paragraphs: Double-height lobbies and atriums are where commercial trees earn their size. A 16 to 20 foot tree under a skylight in a corporate atrium or a mall concourse is a landmark for the whole building. People meet at it, photograph it and remember it. It is also the hardest tree to get right.

Tall trees are installed from an indoor-rated lift, in sections, and decorated from the lift as well. We check floor loading, lift access through doors and corridors, and the ceiling structure around the top of the tree. Power needs are modest because the tree is pre-lit with commercial LED strings, but the circuit needs to be dedicated and accessible.

In an atrium, the decoration has to read from upper floors looking down as well as from the lobby looking up. Larger ornaments, wider ribbon and a strong topper are what make a 20 foot tree look finished rather than busy. This is also where leasing makes the most sense, because a tree this size is a serious piece of product to own and store.

sections.heading: What we check on the site visit
paragraphs: Bring a tape measure and these questions to your own lobby walk, and we will confirm them on ours. Height to the lowest obstruction. Clear floor circle. Distance from the entrance and whether the tree is on the main axis. Nearest outlet and whether it is on its own circuit. Route a lift or a tall tree section would take from the loading dock.

We also ask how the lobby is used in December. Hotels hold events and photos. Office towers have tenant parties. Condos have residents coming and going with parcels. The right tree size respects all of that, and the right install window, usually after hours or overnight, keeps the lobby open while we work.

Call 519-266-6796 or send photos and a ceiling height and we will suggest a size and a scheme within one business day. If you would rather see options in the space, we bring ribbon and ornament samples to the site visit and can show you where a 9, 12 or 15 foot tree would stand before anything is ordered.

faqs.question: What size Christmas tree fits a 12 foot lobby ceiling?
faqs.answer: A 9 foot pre-lit tree is the usual choice for a 12 foot ceiling. It leaves comfortable clearance above the topper and has a footprint around 6 feet wide. If the lobby is narrow or busy, a slim-profile 9 foot tree keeps the height with less floor space.

faqs.question: How tall can a commercial lobby Christmas tree be?
faqs.answer: Our pre-lit lobby and atrium trees run from 7 feet up to 20 feet and beyond. Trees over about 12 feet are installed in sections from an indoor lift. The limit is usually ceiling clearance, floor space and lift access through the building rather than the tree itself.

faqs.question: Do you decorate the whole tree or only the visible side?
faqs.answer: It depends on where the tree stands. Trees against a wall are decorated on the visible sides. Trees in the centre of a lobby or atrium, or seen from upper floors, are decorated all the way round. We confirm this at the site visit so the quote reflects it.

title: Hotel Holiday Decor Planning Checklist
metaDescription: Hotel holiday decor checklist: lobby trees, porte-cochère lighting, brand colours, overnight installs, insurance, maintenance and January takedown.
excerpt: A practical checklist for hotel GMs, front office and facilities managers planning Christmas decor: the lobby tree, the porte-cochère and approach, brand colour approval, overnight installs, vendor paperwork, season-long maintenance and January takedown, with a month-by-month table.

sections.heading: Why hotel holiday decor needs its own plan
paragraphs: A hotel is never closed. Guests arrive at midnight, breakfast service starts at six, and the lobby is both the brand and the busiest room in the building. That makes hotel Christmas decorating different from an office tower, where the lobby empties at six, or a plaza, where the work happens in a parking lot.

Hotel decor has to be installed without disrupting arrivals, approved by people who may not be on site, consistent with brand standards and robust enough to survive six weeks of luggage carts, children and holiday parties. It also has to come down cleanly in January while the hotel keeps running.

This checklist is the one we work through with hotel GMs and facilities managers across Southwestern Ontario, the GTA and Hamilton-Niagara. Use it to prepare for the site visit and to brief your own team. It runs in the order the decisions actually happen, from what guests see to who signs off to what the night manager needs to know, and it ends with the part most hotels forget: January.

sections.heading: Step one: decide what the guest should see, in order
paragraphs: Walk the arrival route as a guest. The approach and porte-cochère come first: wrapped trees along the drive, a lit canopy edge, wrapped or lit columns, garland and wreaths at the doors. Then the lobby: the main tree, garland on the reception desk or staircase, a wreath or arch at the entrance. Then the secondary spaces: elevator lobbies, the restaurant or bar entrance, the ballroom foyer.

Rank those in order of guest impact and budget them in that order. If budget is tight, a strong porte-cochère and a strong lobby tree beat a thin scheme spread across every corridor. The elevator lobby and ballroom foyer can be added in a later season under the same agreement.

Photograph each spot now, in daylight and at night, and note ceiling heights, outlets and anything in the way. Those photos and measurements are most of what we need to start a proposal. If you have photos from a previous season, send those too, even if you want a different look this year. They show us the scale and the light.
bullets: Approach and porte-cochère: tree wraps, canopy edge, columns, doors
Lobby: main tree, desk or staircase garland, entrance wreath or arch
Secondary: elevator lobbies, restaurant entrance, ballroom foyer, planters

sections.heading: Step two: get the brand and the budget approved early
paragraphs: Most hotels need sign-off from more than one person: the GM, an owner or management company, and sometimes a brand standards team. Colour schemes are the usual sticking point. Warm white with gold ribbon suits most hotel finishes. Navy and silver or blue and gold read as modern and work well against marble and glass. Red with gold is traditional and festive.

We bring ribbon and ornament samples to the site visit so your team can see them in the lobby's own light rather than on a screen. We can also match a brand colour from a logo or a signage specification. Once the scheme is set it carries through the tree, garland, wreaths and planters. It also means the brand team can approve a physical sample rather than a rendering.

On budget, ask for the lease and purchase options side by side. For hotel lobby trees we recommend leasing: one seasonal price for design, product, install, maintenance, removal and storage, with the option to refresh the scheme in a later year. A multi-year agreement locks the price and dates so the number is known before the budget cycle.

sections.heading: Step three: vendor paperwork and site logistics
paragraphs: Hotels and their management companies usually need a certificate of insurance, WSIB clearance and a vendor setup form before anyone works on site. Ask for those at proposal stage, not install week. Our crews are insured and WSIB-compliant and we provide the documents on request. Having the file complete also makes it easier to add a second hotel in the same portfolio later.

Logistics decide how smooth install night is. Where can a bucket truck or aerial lift park without blocking the porte-cochère? Which outlets will the exterior lighting use and are they on separate circuits? What is the route for a 15 foot tree from the loading dock to the lobby? Who on the night team has the keys and the contact number?

Agree a written install window and a takedown window with the front office. Overnight installs are standard for us at hotels, and the point of the plan is that the morning shift arrives to a finished lobby and an open drive. If the hotel has a blackout period, such as a sold-out weekend or a large conference, tell us at proposal stage.
bullets: Certificate of insurance and WSIB clearance on file
Lift parking, power and tree route confirmed
Night manager briefed with a contact number

sections.heading: The hotel decor timeline
paragraphs: Hotels run on events, and the holiday calendar fills early with corporate parties, weddings and brunches. Work backwards from the first event you want the decor in place for. For most hotels that is late November. The table below shows what has to happen by when, with extra time for approvals built in.

sections.heading: Step four: install night and the first morning
paragraphs: On install night the crew arrives with everything on the truck. Exterior work is usually done first on a separate night so the porte-cochère is only coned for a few hours. The lobby tree goes up in sections, is decorated from a lift if it is tall, and the garland, wreaths and planters follow. Every circuit is tested and every timer set before the crew leaves.

In the morning your team should find a finished display, no packaging, no ladders and a contact number for the season. Walk the lobby with the day manager and send us anything that needs adjusting. Small changes such as a bow moved or a timer shifted are part of the program.

Porte-cochère lighting is on a timer with the rest of the exterior so it comes on at dusk every night without staff involvement. If an event runs late, a phone call changes the timer. paragraphs: Season-long maintenance is included at no charge for any fault. Takedown is overnight in the first three weeks of January. Tell us if you want the lobby back for a specific event or if you would like the warm-white exterior lighting kept as winter lighting into February. Everything is labelled by hotel and location and stored in our warehouse, so your housekeeping storage stays clear.

Before the next budget cycle you will have photos, a note of what worked and a renewal with locked pricing if you are on a multi-year agreement. That is the simplest version of hotel holiday decor: decide once, approve once, and have the lobby look right every year. The lobby looks right every year and nobody has to rediscover the plan.

faqs.question: Can hotel Christmas decor be installed without closing the lobby or the drive?

faqs.question: Can you match our hotel brand colours?

title: Holiday Decorating for Condo Boards and Property Managers
metaDescription: How condo boards and property managers plan holiday decor: lobby trees, entrance lighting, board approval, typical costs, insurance and storage.
excerpt: A guide for condo boards, property managers and superintendents on commissioning holiday decor for a multi-residential building: what to decorate, how to get it through the board, what it typically costs, who does the work, and how to make sure nothing ends up stored in the mechanical room.

sections.heading: Why condo lobbies are different
paragraphs: A condo lobby is a home for hundreds of people and a workplace for a superintendent and a concierge. Holiday decor there has to please residents with different tastes, survive parcel deliveries and movers, meet the corporation's insurance rules and fit a budget approved by a board that meets once a month. It also has to be stored somewhere, which is where most condo decor programs go wrong.

We work with condo boards and property management companies across Southwestern Ontario, the GTA and Hamilton-Niagara on multi-residential holiday decor: lobby and elevator-lobby trees, entrance garland and wreaths, planters at the doors, and exterior lighting on the entrance canopy, columns and landscape trees. Everything is our own inventory, installed, maintained, removed and stored by us.

This guide is for the board member or property manager who has been handed the holiday decor file. It covers what to decorate, how to get it approved, what to expect on price and how the program runs so the superintendent never touches a box of lights. Share it with the rest of the board before the meeting.

sections.heading: What to decorate in a multi-residential building
paragraphs: Start with the two places every resident passes: the front entrance and the lobby. Outside, that usually means a lit canopy edge or roofline over the entrance, wrapped columns, a wreath on the doors and wrapped landscape trees or lit cone trees along the walk. Inside, it means a pre-lit tree sized to the lobby ceiling, garland on the concierge desk or railing, and a wreath or arch at the vestibule.

Elevator lobbies on the ground floor are the natural second step. A smaller tree or lit gift boxes beside the elevators carries the scheme through to where residents wait every day. Amenity rooms and party rooms are a third step if the budget allows, often timed for a residents' holiday event.

Colour matters more in condos than in offices because residents see it daily for six weeks. Warm white with gold or silver accents is the safest choice and matches most lobby finishes. Blue and white reads as winter rather than Christmas, which some boards prefer for a mixed community. We bring samples so the board can decide in the lobby itself.
bullets: Entrance: canopy or roofline, columns, door wreath, wrapped trees or cone trees
Lobby: main tree, desk or railing garland, vestibule wreath or arch
Elevator lobby: small tree or lit gift boxes in the same scheme

sections.heading: Getting it through the board
paragraphs: Boards approve faster when the proposal answers the questions they will ask. What exactly is included. What it costs this year and next. Who is insured for what. Where the product is stored. What happens if something breaks. Our proposals are written to answer all of those on one page, with the lease and purchase options side by side.

Timing is the hard part. If the board meets monthly and the proposal is tabled in September, approval might land in October and the install in November. That works, but the choice of dates is narrower. Aim to have a site visit in July or August and the proposal on the agenda for the September meeting at the latest.

For multi-year agreements, boards like knowing the price and the dates are locked for the term, and that the corporation is not buying product it has to insure and store. That is why most condo lobby trees are leased rather than bought. Insurance and storage are two fewer line items for the corporation to manage.

sections.heading: What condo holiday decor typically costs
paragraphs: Every program is custom quoted, but boards need ranges to set a budget line. As a typical range, a decorated 9 foot pre-lit lobby tree on a seasonal lease commonly starts around $1,500 per season, including install, maintenance, January removal and storage. Adding desk garland, a door wreath and a pair of entrance planters moves the lobby program up from there.

Exterior lighting on a condo entrance, with a lit canopy, wrapped columns and a few wrapped trees, commonly runs from a few thousand dollars per season. A full building program with a double-height lobby tree, elevator lobby decor and an extended exterior scheme can reach five figures. Treat these as typical ranges, not quotes.

The table below lists what moves the price and what a board can do about each item. Share it with the board so the discussion is about scope rather than surprises. Most corporations find the easiest savings in two rows: sizing the tree to the ceiling rather than the biggest one that fits, and lighting the entrance well instead of the whole building thinly.

sections.heading: Who does the work and who is covered
paragraphs: No condo corporation should have a superintendent on a ladder hanging lights over the entrance. Our crews are insured and WSIB-compliant, work from our own bucket trucks and aerial lifts, and provide a certificate of insurance and WSIB clearance for the corporation's file before work starts. Property management companies can add us as a vendor across a portfolio.

We install after hours or in a quiet window so residents, deliveries and visitor parking are not disrupted, and we keep the lobby open while we work. Exterior installs are usually done in October and left off on the timer until the board wants them lit. Interior installs are done in November.

The concierge or superintendent gets a contact number for the season. Any fault in the display, from a dark tree section to a timer knocked off after the time change, is fixed at no charge as part of included maintenance. Nobody in the building needs to test a string, climb a ladder or buy a replacement bulb.

sections.heading: Takedown, storage and the mechanical room problem
paragraphs: The reason many condo decor programs fail after a few years is storage. Trees bought by a previous board end up in the mechanical room, ornaments get crushed, strings fail and the superintendent spends a December weekend testing lights. Then someone proposes buying everything again. The board pays twice and the lobby still looks tired.

Our program removes that cycle. Takedown runs through the first three weeks of January, after hours where needed. Everything is labelled by building and location and stored in our warehouse, tested before the next season and ready to go up on your reserved date. This is included whether you lease the decor or own it and pay for the service program. Storage space in the building goes back to residents.

If the board wants the warm-white exterior lighting kept up as winter lighting into February, say so at quoting time and we will plan the takedown around it. Themed interior decor normally comes down in January. Lit cone trees and wrapped landscape trees are the pieces most often kept as winter lighting because they read as winter rather than Christmas.

sections.heading: A simple path for the board
paragraphs: Here is the whole process in one place. A board member or property manager calls 519-266-6796 or sends a request with photos of the entrance and lobby and a ceiling height. We reply within one business day and book a site visit in summer. The proposal goes to the next board meeting with lease and purchase options, insurance documents and typical install and takedown windows.

Once approved, the agreement is signed, a deposit reserves product and dates, and we confirm access and timing with the property manager and superintendent. Exterior goes in during October, interior in November, maintenance runs through December, takedown and storage in January, and the board gets a renewal with locked pricing if it signed for multiple years.

The corporation sees one invoice per season and nothing in the mechanical room. The superintendent gets a phone number instead of a box of lights. The board gets a number it can approve once and a result residents notice every day in December. That is the version of condo holiday decorating that boards keep renewing.

faqs.question: Who do you invoice for condo holiday decor, the board or the management company?
faqs.answer: Either, depending on how the corporation runs its vendors. Most often we invoice the condominium corporation through the property management company with a purchase order or vendor setup form. One invoice per season covers product, install, maintenance, takedown and storage.

faqs.question: Can the install be done without blocking the entrance or visitor parking?
faqs.answer: Yes. We install after hours or in a quiet window agreed with the property manager, cone off only the area we are working in and keep the lobby and entrance open. Exterior work is usually done in October on a separate visit from the lobby install.

faqs.question: Where is the condo's holiday decor stored between seasons?
faqs.answer: In our warehouse, labelled by building and location, tested before the next season. Storage is included whether the corporation leases the decor or owns it and pays for the service program. Nothing goes into the building's mechanical room or storage lockers.

title: Commercial Christmas Light Installation: Safety, Insurance and What to Ask
metaDescription: What to ask before hiring commercial Christmas light installers in Ontario: insurance, WSIB, lifts, power, timers, after-hours work and maintenance.
excerpt: The questions a property manager, facilities lead or hotel GM should ask before hiring commercial Christmas light installers: insurance and WSIB, bucket trucks and aerial lifts, electrical load and timers, after-hours access, product warranty and who fixes a fault in December. With a vendor checklist table.

sections.heading: Why this matters more on a commercial property
paragraphs: On a house, a fall from a ladder hurts one person. On a commercial property, a fall from a roofline, a lift tipping in a parking lot or an overloaded circuit in a lobby becomes the property's problem: liability, insurance claims, a tenant complaint or an incident report for the board. Commercial Christmas light installation is work at height on a working property, and it should be treated that way.

Most of the risk is managed before anyone arrives on site. The right installer has the right coverage, the right equipment, a plan for access and power, and product that will not fail in January. The wrong installer has a pickup truck, extension ladders and a receipt from a big-box store.

This guide lists what to ask, what the answers should be and why. It is written from the side of the crew that does the work, so it is specific. We are based in London, Ontario and work across Southwestern Ontario, the GTA and Hamilton-Niagara, and these are the questions our clients ask us.

sections.heading: Insurance and WSIB: the paperwork that protects you
paragraphs: Ask for a certificate of insurance naming your property or management company, and ask for a WSIB clearance certificate. In Ontario, a contractor working at height on your property without WSIB coverage can leave the property owner exposed if a worker is injured. Reputable installers provide both documents on request, usually at proposal stage so vendor setup is done before install week.

Our crews are insured and WSIB-compliant and we supply both documents as a matter of course. If an installer hesitates, cannot name their insurer or says they are covered under a home policy, that is your answer. Ask for the documents in writing and keep them with the vendor file for the season.

Also ask who actually does the work. Some companies sell the job and subcontract the install. That is not always a problem, but you need to know whose insurance and WSIB apply to the person on your roof. We install with our own crews. Ask the same question about takedown in January, which is sometimes handed to a different crew.
bullets: Certificate of insurance naming your property
WSIB clearance certificate, current
Confirmation that the installer's own crews do the work

sections.heading: Lifts, ladders and working at height
paragraphs: Rooflines, porte-cochères, canopies, columns and tall trees should be installed from a bucket truck or aerial lift, not from an extension ladder leaning on a gutter. Lifts are safer, faster and let the installer place lights properly along a soffit or wrap a tree all the way up rather than as far as a ladder reaches.

Ask what equipment will be used and where it will be positioned. At the site visit we check ground surface, slope, overhead wires and how to keep walkways and lanes open while the lift is in use. For atrium trees we use indoor-rated lifts and check floor loading and access routes. Lift requirements are a real cost driver, which is why we price them up front rather than discovering them on install day.

Ask about weather limits too. Lifts do not go up in high wind, and roofs are not walked in ice. A good installer will tell you that an October install in mild weather is safer and better than a late-November install in sleet, and will plan the calendar accordingly. That is also why early booking matters.

sections.heading: Power, circuits and timers
paragraphs: Commercial LED strings and C9 LED bulbs draw a small fraction of the power that incandescent product used to, so most storefront and lobby displays run on existing outlets. That does not mean power can be ignored. Ask the installer to map the outlets at the site visit, confirm which circuits they share and identify any run that needs an outlet added by an electrician before install.

Cords should never be run through doors or windows, across walkways without cover, or daisy-chained beyond the rating of the string. Outdoor connections should be weather-rated and off the ground where snow collects. These are basic practices and you should see them on the finished install. If something looks improvised, ask about it before the crew leaves.

Every exterior program should be on timers so staff never switch anything. We set timers on install day, usually dusk to a set time such as 11 pm or midnight, test them, adjust after the time change if needed and check them on maintenance visits. A display that runs all day on a staff switch is wasting power and bulb life. Lobby trees can run on a timer or on a switch at the desk.

sections.heading: Product: whose is it and who warranties it?
paragraphs: Ask what product will be installed and who owns it. Retail light strings are not built for six weeks on a roofline through freezing rain. Commercial-grade LED strings and C9 bulbs with sealed sockets and heavier cord are. The difference shows up in the second week of January when retail product has failed sections and commercial product comes down ready to be reused.

Ask who fixes a failure in December and what it costs. Our answer is that maintenance is included all season at no charge for any fault, because everything we install is our own inventory, tested and tracked. That is also why we do not install customer-supplied lights: we cannot warranty product we did not source.

Finally, ask what happens in January. Takedown should be scheduled, done with the same lifts and crews, and the product should be labelled and stored somewhere that is not your mechanical room. Labelled storage in our warehouse is part of every program. Ask to see the storage, or at least to know where it is and how product is tracked.

paragraphs: Use this table when comparing commercial Christmas light installers. It is the same list a property manager or hotel facilities lead would use for any contractor working at height, applied to holiday lighting. A yes in every row is the baseline, not a bonus. Print it and take it to the site visit.

If a quote is dramatically cheaper than the others, check this table first. The difference is almost always in one of these rows: no lift, retail product, no maintenance, no takedown, or a subcontracted crew whose coverage you cannot see. A fair comparison is only possible when every quote covers the same program from site visit to storage.

sections.heading: What a safe install looks like on the day
paragraphs: On install day the crew arrives with the lift, the product and a plan agreed with your building staff. The work area is coned off and kept as small as possible. Walkways stay open or are rerouted with signage. Cords are routed off the ground and away from doors. Every circuit is tested, every timer is set and the crew walks the display with you or your staff before leaving.

Overnight installs follow the same process with lit lifts and a night contact at the building. The point is that the morning shift, the tenants or the guests arrive to a finished display and nothing else: no ladders, no packaging, no cords across a lobby. A good installer leaves the site cleaner than they found it.

If you want to see how we work before you commit, ask for a site visit. We will walk your property, show you where the lift goes, where the power comes from and what we would do differently from last year. Call 519-266-6796 or send a request and we reply within one business day. Our crews are the people you will meet on the site visit.

faqs.question: Do I need to be on site during a commercial Christmas light install?
faqs.answer: No. We agree access, power and timing with your building staff in advance and work from that plan, including overnight. A night contact with keys and a phone number is enough. We walk the finished display with whoever is available and send photos if nobody is.

faqs.question: Will commercial Christmas lights overload our building's electrical system?
faqs.answer: Rarely. Commercial LED strings and C9 LED bulbs draw a small fraction of what incandescent lights did, so most displays run on existing outlets. We map outlets and circuits at the site visit and tell you clearly if an electrician needs to add an outlet before install.

faqs.question: What if a snowplow or a vandal damages the lights?
faqs.answer: We repair or replace the damaged section as part of included season-long maintenance at no charge. Because the product is our own inventory, replacements match. If damage keeps happening at the same spot, we talk with you about rerouting or protecting that run.

title: How to Budget for Commercial Holiday Decor
metaDescription: How to budget commercial holiday decor in Ontario: typical ranges for lobby trees and exterior lighting, cost drivers, lease vs buy and multi-year pricing.
excerpt: A plain-language guide to budgeting commercial holiday decor for a hotel, office, condo, plaza or municipality: honest typical ranges, the five things that drive price, how leasing and buying change the numbers, what is included, how deposits and invoicing work, and how multi-year agreements make the line predictable.

sections.heading: Start with scope, not a number
paragraphs: The most common budgeting question we get is some version of how much does commercial Christmas light installation cost. The honest answer is that it depends on scope, and the useful answer is that scope is made of five measurable things: linear footage, tree count and height, lift requirements, indoor decor scope and whether you sign for one season or several. Once you know those, the budget follows.

This guide gives typical ranges so you can set a line in a budget before a site visit, then explains each driver so you can move the number up or down on purpose. The ranges are typical for the work we do across Southwestern Ontario, the GTA and Hamilton-Niagara. They are not quotes. A firm price comes from a site visit or from plans and photos.

It also explains what is included in our price, because comparing a turnkey program against a product-only quote is the easiest way to get a budget wrong. A number that leaves out maintenance, takedown and storage is not a lower price, it is a smaller scope, and the missing pieces land on your staff in December and January.

sections.heading: Typical ranges to anchor a budget
paragraphs: For interior work, a decorated 9 foot pre-lit lobby tree on a seasonal lease commonly starts around $1,500 per season, with install, maintenance, January removal and storage included. Taller trees, multiple trees, garland, wreaths and planters move a lobby program up from there. Atrium programs with 16 to 20 foot trees, and shopping mall programs with village displays or Santa photo sets, run to five figures.

For exterior work, a storefront with a lit roofline, wrapped columns and wreaths commonly starts at a few thousand dollars per season. A plaza, hotel exterior or campus with rooflines, porte-cochère lighting, wrapped boulevard and parking-lot trees and lit cone trees typically runs to tens of thousands. Giant outdoor trees and animated pixel light shows are quoted on their own.

Treat all of these as typical ranges. Two plazas with the same square footage can land in very different places depending on how many trees are wrapped and whether a lift is needed for the roofline. The table below lays the same ranges out by program type so you can find the row that looks like your property.

rows: Design, pre-lit tree, ornaments and ribbon, install, maintenance, removal, storage
Taller or multiple trees, desk or railing garland, entrance wreath, planters

sections.heading: The five cost drivers
paragraphs: Linear footage is the biggest exterior driver. Rooflines, canopy edges, columns and walkway borders are priced by the foot, and a long low plaza has a lot of feet. Lighting the entrance and the most visible elevation well usually gives a better result per dollar than a thin line around the entire building.

Tree count and height drive both exterior and interior cost. Wrapping a mature boulevard tree takes more strings and more lift time than a young one. Indoors, a 12 foot lobby tree costs more than a 9 foot one and a 20 foot atrium tree is a different scale of product and labour altogether.

Lift requirements add equipment and time wherever the work is above ladder height or over a canopy. Indoor decor scope, meaning garland, wreaths, planters, arches and custom pieces, is additive and easy to phase. And one season versus multi-year changes the pricing because a multi-year agreement locks the price, holds your product and gives us a predictable schedule.

sections.heading: What is included, and what to compare
paragraphs: Our price is turnkey: design from a site visit, product from our own commercial-grade inventory, installation by insured and WSIB-compliant crews with bucket trucks and aerial lifts, after-hours or overnight timing where needed, season-long maintenance at no charge for any fault, January takedown, labelled storage in our warehouse and priority dates next season. One invoice.

When comparing quotes, line those items up. A quote that covers product and install only leaves maintenance, takedown and storage for someone else, usually your staff. A quote that uses retail product leaves replacement for you in year two. A quote without lifts may not reach your roofline properly. The cheapest number on the page is often the most expensive program.

Ask for the lease and purchase options on the same scope. Leasing is lower in year one and keeps product, ageing and storage on us. Buying costs more in year one and less in later years if the look stays the same. Our guide to lease versus buy covers that choice in detail.

sections.heading: Phasing a program across seasons
paragraphs: You do not have to do everything in year one. Many properties start with the pieces that have the most impact per dollar and add scope at renewal under the same agreement. A hotel might start with the porte-cochère and the lobby tree, then add the ballroom foyer and elevator lobbies the next year. A plaza might light the roofline on the main elevation first and wrap the parking-lot trees later.

Phasing also makes approvals easier. A board or an owner sees a modest number in year one, sees the result, and approves the addition with confidence. Because the product is our inventory, adding scope later does not strand anything you bought. It can be added, refreshed or scaled at renewal without a redesign.

The one thing not to phase is quality. A smaller program done properly with commercial-grade product and a full service program looks better and costs less over time than a larger program done thinly. Start smaller if you must, but start with product that will still light next January and a program that includes someone to fix it.

sections.heading: Deposits, invoicing and the budget cycle
paragraphs: A deposit at signing reserves your install dates and lets us pull product from inventory or order custom pieces. The balance is invoiced after installation, and one invoice covers the whole season: product, install, maintenance, takedown and storage. We work with purchase orders, vendor setup forms and standard commercial payment terms, and we invoice per property or per portfolio for management companies.

For budgeting, that means the holiday decor line is a single annual number with a deposit in late summer or early autumn and the balance in late autumn. Multi-year agreements make the number the same each year for the term, which is what most hotels, management companies and BIAs want.

Site visits and proposals happen from July to September, which lines up with most budget cycles. If your fiscal year starts at a different time, tell us and we will time the proposal and deposit to fit. Multi-year clients get their renewal early enough to put the number in before the cycle closes.

sections.heading: A worked example of how the number moves
paragraphs: Picture a mid-sized office building with a double-height lobby and a short entrance canopy. The core program is a 12 foot leased lobby tree with ribbon and ornaments, garland on the reception desk, a wreath at the entrance and a lit canopy edge with two wrapped trees at the doors. That lands in the low to mid four figures per season as a typical range.

Add a pair of lit accent trees flanking the main tree and a small tree in the elevator lobby, and the interior moves up by a step. Wrap the six boulevard trees along the frontage from a lift and the exterior moves up by another. Sign for three years and the price per season is locked for the term and the install dates are the same every year.

Those are the levers. Decide which elevations and spaces matter most, size the trees to the ceilings, let us price the lift requirements honestly and choose the term that fits your approvals. Call 519-266-6796 or send plans and photos and we will reply with a proposal within one business day.

faqs.question: How much should a hotel budget for Christmas decor?
faqs.answer: As a typical range, a hotel with a leased lobby tree, desk or staircase garland and porte-cochère lighting with approach tree wraps often lands in the mid four to low five figures per season, everything included. Larger lobbies, more trees and longer rooflines move it up. We quote firm from a site visit.

faqs.question: Does the price include takedown and storage?
faqs.answer: Yes. Every program includes January takedown and labelled storage in our warehouse, along with season-long maintenance at no charge for any fault. That is true whether you lease the decor or buy it and pay for the service program. One invoice covers the season.

faqs.question: Is a multi-year agreement cheaper than booking each year?
faqs.answer: It locks the price for the term, so you are protected from increases, and it gives you priority install dates and reserved product. The main value is predictability for budgeting and scheduling. If you want to add scope mid-term, we quote the addition and leave the rest as is.
